examples.question_text: A quantity is modelled by $Q=18e^{-0.4t}$. Verify that it satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-0.4Q$, and state its initial value.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=-0.4\times18e^{-0.4t}\\&=-0.4Q\end{align*}$

The model satisfies the differential equation.

$\begin{align*}Q(0)&=18e^0\\&=18\end{align*}$

examples.question_text: A radioactive sample initially has mass $120$ grams. Its mass decreases at a rate proportional to the mass present, with decay constant of magnitude $0.07$ per day. Write a differential equation and a formula for its mass $M$ after $t$ days.
examples.solution_text:
The mass decreases, so $k=-0.07$ per day.

$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.07M$

Using $M=Ae^{kt}$, the initial mass gives $A=120$.

$M=120e^{-0.07t}$ grams, for $t\ge0$.

examples.question_text: The mass $M$ of a sample satisfies $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=kM$, where $t$ is measured in minutes. When its mass is $320$ grams, it is decreasing at $24$ grams per minute. Find $k$ and the rate of change when its mass is $100$ grams.
examples.solution_text:
The signed rate is $-24$ grams per minute.

$\begin{align*}-24&=320k\\k&=-\dfrac{24}{320}\\&=-0.075\end{align*}$

Thus $k=-0.075$ per minute.

When $M=100$ grams:

$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dM}{dt}&=-0.075\times100\\&=-7.5\text{ g/min}\end{align*}$

The mass is decreasing at $7.5$ grams per minute.

examples.question_text: Two positive quantities have models $G=30e^{0.2t}$ and $D=30e^{-0.2t}$ for $t\ge0$. Sketch both on the same axes. Explain why the growth curve becomes steeper while the decay curve becomes less steep, and identify the decay curve's horizontal asymptote.
For $k\ne0$, determine when $Q=Ae^{kt}+B$ satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$. Hence explain why $Q=14e^{0.3t}+5$ does not satisfy an equation of the form $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=cQ$ for any constant $c$.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=kAe^{kt}\\&=k(Q-B)\\&=kQ-kB\end{align*}$

This equals $kQ$ exactly when $kB=0$. Since $k\ne0$, it requires $B=0$.

For $Q=14e^{0.3t}+5$:

$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=4.2e^{0.3t}\\&=0.3(Q-5)\\&=0.3Q-1.5\end{align*}$

If this were $cQ$, then $(0.3-c)Q=1.5$ for all $t$. The quantity $Q$ varies with $t$, so no constant $c$ can satisfy this identity.

examples.question_text: A quantity has model $Q=-80e^{0.15t}$ for $t\ge0$. Find its initial value and proportionality constant. Explain whether $Q$ increases or decreases as time passes.
examples.solution_text:
$\begin{align*}Q(0)&=-80e^0\\&=-80\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}\dfrac{dQ}{dt}&=-12e^{0.15t}\\&=0.15Q\end{align*}$

Thus $A=-80$ and $k=0.15$. Since $Q<0$, the rate $0.15Q$ is negative. The quantity decreases, becoming more negative and moving farther from zero.

examples.derivation: Differentiating 18e^(-0.4t) gives -7.2e^(-0.4t)=-0.4Q. At t=0, Q=18. Both requested results are correct.
Decreasing positive mass requires k=-0.07 per day. Thus dM/dt=-0.07M. The initial condition M(0)=120 gives M=120e^(-0.07t) grams for t≥0.
The signed rate gives -24=320k, hence k=-24/320=-0.075 per minute. At M=100 grams, dM/dt=-0.075(100)=-7.5 g/min, a decrease of 7.5 grams per minute.

G(0)=D(0)=30. G'=0.2G is positive and increases as G increases. D'=-0.2D is negative, while its magnitude decreases as D decreases. D tends to zero from above. The plotted functions match both models; at t=5 they are approximately 81.55 and 11.04, within the stated axes. Curve labels identify the correct branches.

Differentiating Ae^(kt)+B gives kAe^(kt)=kQ-kB. Equality with kQ requires kB=0, so B=0 when k≠0. For 14e^(0.3t)+5, the derivative is 4.2e^(0.3t)=0.3Q-1.5. Equality with cQ would require (0.3-c)Q=1.5 for every t, impossible because Q is nonconstant.
Q(0)=-80. Differentiation gives Q'=-12e^(0.15t)=0.15Q, so k=0.15. Since Q remains negative, Q'<0; the quantity decreases and its magnitude increases.
